title: Knowledge Check 2 - Lessons 6-10
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 6-10 - Permissions to Standard Objects, Custom Objects, and Fields. Pass with 80% or higher to move toward unlocking the cert prep exam.

questions.question: A developer writes a Lightning action that returns Account records with a Compensation field. Managers can see it, reps cannot. What is the minimal robust fix?
options: Remove the field from the page layout
Add WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED to the query or strip inaccessible fields before returning
Make the class 'without sharing'
Set the OWD to Private
questions.explanation: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED / stripInaccessible make the code honor FLS for the calling user, so reps receive the field stripped. Layouts and OWD do not make Apex honor field visibility.

questions.question: Which statement about Apex sharing and field-level security is TRUE?
options: A 'without sharing' class automatically enforces field-level security
Apex in user mode must explicitly check field accessibility because SOQL does not enforce FLS by default
WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED returns hidden fields but marks them read-only
Field accessibility cannot be checked in Apex
questions.explanation: Plain SOQL does not filter hidden fields; the developer must add WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED or Schema accessibility checks. System mode does not auto-enforce FLS, and WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED errors rather than silently returning hidden fields.

questions.question: What is the correct layered approach to protect a sensitive field end-to-end?
options: Hide it in FLS and also validate field accessibility in Apex, plus keep layouts consistent
Only remove it from the page layout
Only rely on the org-wide default
Set the field to read-only in FLS only
questions.explanation: Defense in depth pairs FLS (hide) with programmatic enforcement (WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED / accessibility checks) and UI consistency. Any single layer alone leaves a leak surface.

questions.question: A customer stores credit-card numbers and wants to minimize exposure if a backup or export leaks. Which control specifically protects data at rest?
options: Hide the field with FLS
Set OWD to Private
Shield Platform Encryption on the card field
Remove the field from page layouts
questions.explanation: Shield Platform Encryption encrypts the field at rest so leaked/exported data is unusable. FLS, OWD, and layouts restrict which users can see it but do not protect the underlying stored data.

questions.question: Which combination best protects a PII field end to end?
options: Classify it, hide via FLS, encrypt with Shield, and audit changes with field history
Only make the field read-only
Only change the record type
Only set the org-wide default to Private
questions.explanation: Layered protection - classify, restrict (FLS), encrypt at rest (Shield), and audit (field history) - is the model for sensitive data. Any single declarative change leaves a gap.

questions.question: Why does enabling Shield Platform Encryption alone NOT stop an internal user from seeing a sensitive field?
options: Encryption prevents all access
Encryption protects data at rest but does not restrict which authorized users can read the field
Shield only works on standard fields
FLS disables encryption
questions.explanation: Encryption is about protecting stored data from exposure/breach; user visibility is governed by FLS and sharing, which must be configured separately.

questions.question: Only HR managers should ever see records flagged with the custom field Sensitive__c = true; OWD is Public Read Only. Which declarative control delivers this?
options: A sharing rule granting HR managers access
A restriction rule on Sensitive__c = true granting only the HR managers group
Setting the OWD to Private
Field-level security on Sensitive__c
questions.explanation: A restriction rule narrows the publicly visible set to only the HR managers group, blocking everyone else from the flagged records. A sharing rule would GRANT access and cannot remove it, and FLS/OWD do not filter by record criteria.

questions.question: What is TRUE about restriction rules?
options: They can grant record access to a group
They only restrict access to a subset of records based on criteria
They override field-level security
They require Apex Managed Sharing
questions.explanation: Restriction rules only restrict, applying criteria to carve out a sensitive subset. They do not grant, do not touch FLS, and are fully declarative.

questions.question: Which control most directly reduces the blast radius of aged PII records that are no longer needed?
options: A data retention policy that deletes the records after the retention horizon
Changing the profile license
Granting View All
Enabling more app tabs
questions.explanation: A retention policy removes aged PII entirely, shrinking breach scope. License changes, View All, and extra tabs do not reduce exposure of the aged data.

questions.question: A developer must return Case records to a Lightning component but hide any fields the calling user cannot read. Which is the correct pattern?
options: Return the full records and let the UI hide fields
Use Security.stripInaccessible(AccessType.READABLE, cases) before returning
Run the query in a 'without sharing' class
Turn the fields read-only
questions.explanation: stripInaccessible removes unreadable fields per the running user's FLS before the data reaches the client. Returning full records leaks them, 'without sharing' ignores record sharing, and UI hiding is not security.

questions.question: Why does WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED sometimes throw an exception for a query that runs fine without it?
options: The object has too many fields
A selected field or object is not readable by the running user, and the enforcement is all-or-nothing
The query contains a formula field
The class is 'with sharing'
questions.explanation: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED is strict: any inaccessible field in the SELECT list raises an error rather than returning partial data. This is expected, intended behavior, not a bug.

questions.question: Which is the recommended way to guard an insert from an inbound form so users cannot write fields they lack FLS for?
options: Insert the raw payload
Security.stripInaccessible(AccessType.CREATABLE, payload) before insert
Make the class 'without sharing'
Add the fields to a page layout
questions.explanation: Strip CREATABLE fields before DML so only fields the user is allowed to create/update are persisted, closing the mass-assignment FLS gap.

questions.question: A batch job must modify records owned by users across many divisions, regardless of ownership, using a queueable that runs as the system. Which class declaration is appropriate and why?
options: 'with sharing' so sharing rules apply
'without sharing' (or default system mode) because the operation is platform-context and must ignore record ownership
A permission set with View All
runAs(someUser)
questions.explanation: A platform-triggered queueable that must act across ownership boundaries runs in system mode, which ignores record-level sharing. 'with sharing' would restrict it, and permissions/runAs do not change system-mode processing.

questions.question: What does System.runAs(testUser) accomplish in a test?
options: It disables sharing enforcement
It runs the code as testUser so you can assert that user's effective record and field access
It grants testUser Modify All
It only works on the system user
questions.explanation: runAs changes the running user within the test so you can verify the security model from that user's perspective. It does not disable sharing, grant permissions, or require the system user.

questions.question: When is Apex Managed Sharing the correct tool rather than a sharing rule?
options: When the access criteria are too complex or dynamic for a criteria-based sharing rule
When you need to grant object-level permissions
When OWD is Public Read/Write
When you want to restrict access
questions.explanation: Managed Sharing is for complex/dynamic record grants the declarative sharing model cannot express. It grants record access, never object permissions, and cannot restrict.
